sections.normalized_html: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin [MATH: O] with acceleration, measured in [MATH: \textrm m / \textrm s^2,] given by the function [MATH: a(t) = 3t^2+2t-6,] where [MATH: t > 0] is the time in seconds. The positive direction is left to right. If the particle is stationary when [MATH: t=0\,\textrm s,] determine the time intervals in which the particle is moving to the right.

The positive direction is left to right. If the particle is stationary when [MATH: t=0\,\textrm s,] determine the time intervals in which the particle is moving to the right.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we find [MATH: v(t)] by integrating the acceleration with respect to time: [MATH: v(t)|= ∫a(t)dt; = ∫(3t^{2} + 2t − 6)dt; = t^{3} + t^{2} − 6t + C]

We're told that the particle is stationary at the time [MATH: t=0.] This means [MATH: v(0) = 0,] so we have [MATH: 0|= (0)^{3} + (0)^{2} − 6(0) + C; 0|= C,]

and therefore the velocity of the particle is

[MATH: v(t) = t^3+t^2-6t.]

To find the time interval in which the particle is moving to the right, we must solve the inequality [MATH: v > 0.] This gives

[MATH: t^3+t^2-6t = t(t+3)(t-2) > 0.]

Plotting the graph of [MATH: v(t),] we get the following picture.

The particle moves to the right when [MATH: v(t)] is positive. So, from the graph, we see that the particle moves to the right when [MATH: t>2.]

items.title: Finding the Times at Which a Particle Reaches Its Maximum Velocity

sections.normalized_html: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin [MATH: O] with acceleration, measured in [MATH: \textrm m / \textrm s^2,] given by the function [MATH: a(t) = 6t-3t^2,] where [MATH: t>0] is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity [MATH: v=2\,\textrm m / \textrm s] when [MATH: t=1\,\textrm s,] calculate the maximum velocity [MATH: v_{\text{max}}] of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
sections.readable_text: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin [MATH: O] with acceleration, measured in [MATH: \textrm m / \textrm s^2,] given by the function [MATH: a(t) = 6t-3t^2,] where [MATH: t>0] is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity [MATH: v=2\,\textrm m / \textrm s] when [MATH: t=1\,\textrm s,] calculate the maximum velocity [MATH: v_{\text{max}}] of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The extrema of the velocity [MATH: v] occur at the critical points of [MATH: v.]

Since [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d t} = a(t),] to find the times where [MATH: v] is a maximum, we just need to solve [MATH: a(t) = 0] and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving [MATH: a(t) = 0] gives

[MATH: a(t)|= 0; 6t − 3t^{2}|= 0; 3t(2 − t)|= 0; t|= 0, 2.]

Since [MATH: t> 0], the extremum of the velocity function occurs when [MATH: t = 2\,\textrm s.]

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of [MATH: v(t)] and evaluate it at [MATH: t=2\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: v^{″}(t)|= (d^{2}v)/(dt^{2}); = (d)/(dt)((dv)/(dt)); = (d)/(dt)(a(t)); = (d)/(dt)(6t − 3t^{2}); = 6 − 6t; v^{″}(2)|= 6 − 6(2); = − 6] Since [MATH: v''(2) < 0,] we conclude that the velocity is maximized when [MATH: t=2\,\textrm s.]

Now, we find [MATH: v(t)] by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

[MATH: v(t)|= ∫a(t)dt; = ∫(6t − 3t^{2})dt; = 3t^{2} − t^{3} + C]

To determine [MATH: C], we use the fact that [MATH: v(1) = 2.] Substituting this into the above gives [MATH: 3(1)^{2} − (1)^{3} + C|= 2; 3 − 1 + C|= 2⟹C = 0.]

Therefore, the velocity [MATH: v] of the particle at time [MATH: t] is [MATH: v(t) =3t^2-t^3.]

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

[MATH: v_{\text{max}}= v(2) = 3(2)^2 - (2)^3 =4\,\textrm m / \textrm s]

So the maximum velocity [MATH: v_{\text{max}}=4\,\textrm m / \textrm s] is reached at [MATH: t=2\,\textrm s.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Given the acceleration of a particle moving along a straight line relative to a fixed origin [MATH: O,] we can find many characteristics of the particle.

Content:
Let the positive direction be left to right. Suppose the particle has acceleration, measured in [MATH: \textrm{m}/\textrm{s}^2,] given by the function [MATH: a(t) = 6-6t], where [MATH: t > 0] is the time in seconds, and is stationary when [MATH: t=0\,\textrm{s}.]

Content:
Recall we can find the velocity [MATH: v(t)] by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

Content:
[MATH: v(t)|= ∫a(t)dt; = ∫(6 − 6t)dt; = 6t − 3t^{2} + C]

Content:
Since the particle is stationary at the time [MATH: t=0,] we know that [MATH: v(0)=0,] so we have

Content:
[MATH: 0|= 6(0) − 3(0)^{2} + C; 0|= C,]

Content:
and therefore the velocity of the particle is

Content:
[MATH: v(t) = 6t - 3t^2 = 3t(2-t).]

Content:
Plotting the graph of [MATH: v(t),] we get the following picture.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/4d2b223a2a03aca75d47e706b92ef477]

Content:
From the resulting velocity function [MATH: v] and its graph, we can find some characteristics of the particle.

Content:
- Time intervals in which the particle is moving in the positive direction.

Remember that the particle moves to the right (the positive direction) when its velocity is positive, [MATH: v(t) > 0.] So, from the graph, we see that the particle moves to the right when [MATH: 0 < t < 2.]
- Time intervals in which the particle is moving in the negative direction.

Also remember that the particle moves to the left (the negative direction) when its velocity is negative, [MATH: v(t) < 0.] So, from the graph, we see that the particle moves to the left when [MATH: t > 2.]
- Moments when the particle is stationary.

The particle is stationary when [MATH: v = 0 \,\textrm{m}/\textrm{s}{:}]
[MATH: v(t)|= 0; 6t − 3t^{2}|= 0; 3t(2 − t)|= 0]
Therefore, the particle is stationary when [MATH: t=0\,\textrm{s}] and [MATH: t=2\,\textrm{s}.]
- Moments when the velocity of the particle is maximal.

The maximum velocity [MATH: v_\text{max}] of the particle occurs at the maximum of the velocity function [MATH: v.] From calculus, we know that the extrema of [MATH: v] occur at the critical points of [MATH: v.]

Since [MATH: v'(t) = a(t),] to find the times where [MATH: v] is a maximum, we just need to solve [MATH: a(t)=0] and test each solution using the first or second derivative test. Solving [MATH: a(t)=0] gives
[MATH: a(t)|= 0; 6 − 6t|= 0; 6|= 6t; t|= 1.]
We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of and evaluate it at [MATH: t=1{:}]
[MATH: v^{″}(t)|= a^{′}(t); = − 6; v^{″}(1)|= − 6]
Since [MATH: v''(1) < 0,] we conclude that the velocity is maximized when [MATH: t=1\,\textrm{s}.] Therefore, the maximum velocity is
[MATH: v_\text{max} = v(1) = 6(1) - 3(1)^2 = 3\,\textrm{m}/\textrm{s}.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding the Time Intervals on which a Particle is Moving in a Particular Direction

Example Prompt:
A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin [MATH: O] with acceleration, measured in [MATH: \textrm m / \textrm s^2,] given by the function [MATH: a(t) = 3t^2+2t-6,] where [MATH: t > 0] is the time in seconds. The positive direction is left to right. If the particle is stationary when [MATH: t=0\,\textrm s,] determine the time intervals in which the particle is moving to the right.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we find [MATH: v(t)] by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:
[MATH: v(t)|= ∫a(t)dt; = ∫(3t^{2} + 2t − 6)dt; = t^{3} + t^{2} − 6t + C]

We're told that the particle is stationary at the time [MATH: t=0.] This means [MATH: v(0) = 0,] so we have
[MATH: 0|= (0)^{3} + (0)^{2} − 6(0) + C; 0|= C,]

and therefore the velocity of the particle is

[MATH: v(t) = t^3+t^2-6t.]

To find the time interval in which the particle is moving to the right, we must solve the inequality [MATH: v > 0.] This gives

[MATH: t^3+t^2-6t = t(t+3)(t-2) > 0.]

Plotting the graph of [MATH: v(t),] we get the following picture.

[IMG: /graphics/8f7445db34aa0dcfa29db94a8442208a]

The particle moves to the right when [MATH: v(t)] is positive. So, from the graph, we see that the particle moves to the right when [MATH: t>2.]

Item 5 — Example: Finding the Times at Which a Particle Reaches Its Maximum Velocity

Example Prompt:
A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin [MATH: O] with acceleration, measured in [MATH: \textrm m / \textrm s^2,] given by the function [MATH: a(t) = 6t-3t^2,] where [MATH: t>0] is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity [MATH: v=2\,\textrm m / \textrm s] when [MATH: t=1\,\textrm s,] calculate the maximum velocity [MATH: v_{\text{max}}] of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The extrema of the velocity [MATH: v] occur at the critical points of [MATH: v.]

Since [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d t} = a(t),] to find the times where [MATH: v] is a maximum, we just need to solve [MATH: a(t) = 0] and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving [MATH: a(t) = 0] gives

[MATH: a(t)|= 0; 6t − 3t^{2}|= 0; 3t(2 − t)|= 0; t|= 0, 2.]

Since [MATH: t> 0], the extremum of the velocity function occurs when [MATH: t = 2\,\textrm s.]

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of [MATH: v(t)] and evaluate it at [MATH: t=2\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: v^{″}(t)|= (d^{2}v)/(dt^{2}); = (d)/(dt)((dv)/(dt)); = (d)/(dt)(a(t)); = (d)/(dt)(6t − 3t^{2}); = 6 − 6t; v^{″}(2)|= 6 − 6(2); = − 6]
Since [MATH: v''(2) < 0,] we conclude that the velocity is maximized when [MATH: t=2\,\textrm s.]

Now, we find [MATH: v(t)] by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

[MATH: v(t)|= ∫a(t)dt; = ∫(6t − 3t^{2})dt; = 3t^{2} − t^{3} + C]

To determine [MATH: C], we use the fact that [MATH: v(1) = 2.] Substituting this into the above gives
[MATH: 3(1)^{2} − (1)^{3} + C|= 2; 3 − 1 + C|= 2⟹C = 0.]

Therefore, the velocity [MATH: v] of the particle at time [MATH: t] is [MATH: v(t) =3t^2-t^3.]

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

[MATH: v_{\text{max}}= v(2) = 3(2)^2 - (2)^3 =4\,\textrm m / \textrm s]

So the maximum velocity [MATH: v_{\text{max}}=4\,\textrm m / \textrm s] is reached at [MATH: t=2\,\textrm s.]
